metadata.title: How Does Claude Build an Accrual Schedule?
metadata.purpose: Answer whether Claude decides, using its own accounting judgment, which expenses and revenues to accrue at period end -- or is doing something narrower. Lands the carry-out that a drafted accrual JE is a computed entry tied to cited support, waiting for a controller's approval, not Claude's judgment about what you owe.
metadata.source_note: Source sheet's narration carries real skill-specific facts (not unfilled template placeholders) -- see QUESTION.md. Facts preserved: the accrual-schedule skill builds the period-end accrual schedule; for each accrual it computes the entry, cites the support, and drafts the JE; used during month-end close; the JE is a draft for controller approval, not a posting. Register re-registered Teardown -> Plain; source's B03 design-tell verdict became a plain mechanism + both-directions beat; a wrong-guess beat and an anchor (a December utility bill: identified -> computed -> cited -> drafted -> stopped, waiting) were added per hai-simple's Phase 1 structure, since the source's Teardown shape carried neither.

beats.narration_text: Someone types 'What decides an accrual — judgment?' and hesitates, because that's the wrong verb. Liam here, standing in for Bear. Let me show you what the skill actually does.

beats.narration_text: Natural guess: Claude decides, using accounting judgment, which expenses and revenues belong in this period's accrual schedule. It doesn't. Here's what's actually happening — for each accrual, the skill computes the entry and cites the document that backs it. Hand it an expense with no supporting paper and it won't invent a number: nothing to cite, so nothing to draft. They optimized for auditability at the cost of coverage. Smaller list you can defend, not a bigger list you can't.

shot.new_visual_element: An accountant-judgment figure weighing what to accrue, struck through; a written compute/cite/draft procedure lit instead

production_viz.label: Judgment, struck -- compute/cite/draft, lit
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a figure icon labelled 'ACCOUNTING JUDGMENT' beside a thought-bubble of scattered decision marks. Right: a numbered card labelled 'COMPUTE / CITE / DRAFT'. The judgment side dims and gets a terracotta strike; the procedure side stays lit. A final line reads 'no document -- not on the list' and the figure does not reach for it.

beats.narration_text: The actual machinery — three moves per accrual: compute the entry, cite the supporting document, draft the journal entry. Nothing beyond that. Watch the anchor: a December utility bill that won't be invoiced until January. Identified. Entry computed from the contract terms. Contract cited as the support. Draft JE created. Then it halts. Notice the choice — the stopping point is a design decision, not a limit. The whole shape says 'controller's desk next,' not 'ledger next.'

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- a December utility bill traveling identified -> computed -> cited -> drafted, then stopping

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one accrual, four stops
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Four stacked cards labelled 'IDENTIFIED', 'ENTRY COMPUTED', 'SUPPORT CITED', 'JE DRAFTED'. A single highlighted token 'DEC. UTILITY BILL' travels down through all four cards in turn, each lighting as it arrives. At the bottom, the token halts beside a label 'awaiting approval' -- it does not continue past the drafted card. THIS EXACT COMPOSITION RETURNS, PAID OFF, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: The draft is built — computed, cited, ready to review. Now the honest part. A drafted JE with a citation isn't a correct entry — the draft only reflects what the cited document says, and a wrong document produces a wrong entry, cited correctly. Runs the other direction too: an accrual with no draft this period doesn't mean the skill broke; it can mean that expense has no qualifying support yet. This works if you value defensible entries you'll re-check; it fails if you wanted the machine to catch bad source documents on its own. Either way, the draft still waits for a controller before anything posts.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS, drafted and waiting; splits into 'cited is not correct' and 'no draft is not broken'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- drafted, then split
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 FOUR-CARD COMPOSITION RETURNS, identical placement, the token resting at the 'JE DRAFTED' card beside 'awaiting approval'. It shrinks and slides up. Two cards fade in beneath: left reads 'CITED: OK' with a checkmark, then a struck-through 'CORRECT?' beneath it, labelled 'cited is not correct'; right reads 'NO DRAFT' beside a faint 'no support yet' note, labelled 'no draft is not broken'.

beats.narration_text: A drafted accrual JE isn't Claude's judgment about what you owe — it's a computed entry, tied to cited support, waiting for a controller's approval before anything posts.

beats.narration_text: Your turn — here's the prompt, read it with me. Give Claude one expense that belongs in this period's close, with the invoice or contract as its support, and run the accrual-schedule skill: compute the entry, cite that document, draft the JE. Then remove the supporting document, ask for the same accrual again, and watch what happens when the evidence is gone. You're not testing Claude's judgment — you're testing whether the skill stops when there's nothing left to cite. Liam, in for Bear.

beats.narration_text: Here's a prompt you can paste directly into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini — no CLI, no skill install, no accounting software. It asks the model to explain what an accrual actually is and to walk through one concrete example — an unbilled year-end utility expense — showing the draft journal entry, the document that would be cited as its support, and why an accountant would insist on that citation before anything posts. Go deeper: which accruals are hardest to build this way — where the number is real but no single document supports it — and how would a controller handle those?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand what an accrual is in accounting and why a company might want an AI to draft accrual journal entries only from cited source documents rather than from its own judgment about what the company owes. Explain the general accrual concept in one paragraph, then walk through one concrete example — an unbilled utility expense at year-end — showing what the draft journal entry would look like, what document would be cited as its supporting evidence, and why an accountant would insist on that citation before the entry is posted.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: which kinds of accruals are hardest to build this way — where the number is real but no single document supports it cleanly — and how would a controller handle those cases so they still get onto the schedule?
